text:
In the medieval Christian imagination, geography was not a neutral science but a theological declaration. Maps were less navigational instruments than visual encyclopaedias of sacred cosmology.
A class of maps that flourished in European monasteries between roughly the 7th and 14th centuries divided the known world into three continents: Asia occupying the entire upper half, with Europe and Africa split across the lower half. The divisions were formed by bodies of water arranged in the shape of a capital letter — a shape that, combined with the circular ocean frame, gave the entire format a tidy two-character shorthand. The Holy City sat precisely at the centre, not because it was geographically central, but because it was spiritually paramount. East, not north, was at the top — because that was the direction of paradise, of the rising sun, of Eden.
The largest and most magnificent surviving example, made around 1300 and still housed in Hereford Cathedral, stretches over five feet tall and contains more than 500 drawings of cities, animals, biblical scenes, and legendary creatures. A sailor would have laughed at it. A theologian would have found it complete.
What is the Latin name for this type of medieval world map, literally meaning "map of the world"? And what two-character shorthand describes the map's distinctive internal structure?
